title: Roper's Witch Craze: Gender, Psychoanalysis, and the Body in Witch Prosecution
description: Lyndal Roper published Witch Craze: Terror and Fantasy in Baroque Germany in 2004, bringing psychoanalytic and gender-historical approaches to the German witch trials and arguing that the fantasies produced in witch confessions — particularly those involving old women killing infants, destroying potency, and corrupting the young — reflected deep anxieties about female bodily power rooted in the life cycle of maternity, aging, and death. Roper focused particularly on the figure of the lying-in maid accused of murdering the infant she cared for, arguing that post-partum anxieties were projected onto older women in a structure of maternal ambivalence. Her work contributed to ongoing debates about why women made up approximately 75–80 percent of the accused.
historiographical_note: Roper's psychoanalytic approach was controversial: critics questioned whether psychoanalytic frameworks could be applied to early modern subjects across a four-century temporal gap. Defenders argued that the fantasies recorded in confessions demand psychological as well as social explanation, and that Roper's approach illuminated dimensions of witch prosecution that purely social or intellectual historical approaches missed. Her work represents a third tradition alongside the social history of Thomas/Macfarlane and the intellectual history of Clark.
source_method: Roper, Witch Craze: Terror and Fantasy in Baroque Germany (2004); Bamberg and Augsburg trial records; secondary scholarship
